questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes pharmacokinetics from pharmacodynamics?
choices: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug; pharmacodynamics describes what the drug does to the body
Pharmacokinetics describes receptor response only; pharmacodynamics describes renal excretion only
Pharmacokinetics applies only to oral drugs; pharmacodynamics applies only to IV drugs
The two terms have identical meanings
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics covers absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion. Pharmacodynamics covers drug-target interactions and the resulting therapeutic and adverse effects.

questions.question: Why can an oral dose differ from an IV dose of the same medication?
choices: Oral absorption and first-pass metabolism may reduce systemic bioavailability
Every oral medication has exactly 100% bioavailability
IV medication must first be absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract
Route has no effect on concentration over time
questions.explanation: IV medication enters systemic circulation directly. Oral medication may be incompletely absorbed and may undergo intestinal and hepatic first-pass metabolism, so routes are not automatically interchangeable milligram for milligram.

questions.question: Which new finding most increases concern for accumulation of a primarily renally eliminated medication?
choices: A rapid decline in kidney function with increasing adverse effects
A stable kidney trend and expected therapeutic response
A normal room temperature
An unchanged meal preference
questions.explanation: Reduced renal clearance can lengthen half-life and raise exposure when dosing continues unchanged. A rapid kidney decline plus toxicity cues requires prompt assessment and clarification.

questions.question: A medication follows ordinary first-order elimination and has a half-life of 8 hours. Which statement is the best approximation?
choices: Repeated dosing usually approaches steady state after roughly 32 to 40 hours
Steady state occurs immediately after the first dose
The entire drug amount is removed after exactly 8 hours
Half-life is unrelated to accumulation
questions.explanation: A practical approximation is four to five half-lives to approach steady state, so an 8-hour half-life suggests about 32 to 40 hours. Client and drug factors can alter this estimate.

questions.question: Which statement best compares loading and maintenance doses?
choices: A loading dose reaches a target concentration sooner; maintenance dosing replaces drug eliminated over time
A loading dose is always smaller than every maintenance dose
Maintenance dosing is unrelated to clearance
Loading and maintenance doses always use identical calculations
questions.explanation: Loading dose is mainly related to the target concentration and volume of distribution. Maintenance dosing is strongly influenced by clearance, bioavailability, and the desired exposure.

questions.question: A client with low albumin develops toxicity while receiving a highly protein-bound medication, although the reported total drug level is within its usual range. Which hypothesis is most plausible?
choices: The active unbound fraction may be increased despite the ordinary total level
Protein binding cannot affect medication response
A total serum level always measures only unbound drug
Low albumin guarantees reduced medication effect
questions.explanation: For some highly protein-bound drugs, reduced binding can increase the free, active fraction. Sampling time, symptoms, organ function, and drug-specific interpretation remain essential.

questions.question: A trough level is prescribed for a medication. Which plan is generally appropriate?
choices: Verify the drug-specific instructions and obtain the specimen immediately before the scheduled dose
Collect it at any convenient time without documenting the last dose
Collect it during the first minute of an infusion
Skip verification because all trough timing is identical
questions.explanation: A trough is generally drawn just before a dose, but exact instructions are drug specific. Last-dose, infusion, and specimen times must be verified and documented for meaningful interpretation.

questions.question: The RN receives an extended-release tablet for a client whose feeding tube cannot accept whole tablets. What is the best action?
choices: Do not crush it; verify the formulation and request a safe alternative plan
Crush it automatically because all tablets are tube compatible
Dissolve it in the entire feeding bag without checking guidance
Double the dose to compensate for the tube
questions.explanation: Crushing an extended-release product can destroy its release mechanism and cause dose dumping or toxicity. The RN should verify product-specific guidance and clarify an appropriate alternative.

questions.question: Which evaluation best demonstrates safe assessment of medication effectiveness?
choices: Reassess the intended clinical endpoint and predictable adverse effects at the appropriate time
Assume administration proves the medication worked
Evaluate only whether the client swallowed the dose
Ignore laboratory and functional trends if no rash occurs
questions.explanation: Medication evaluation includes whether the intended outcome occurred and whether adverse effects developed. Timing and the relevant clinical, functional, vital-sign, and laboratory endpoints matter.

questions.question: A client taking several medications develops marked sedation and slow respirations after a new sedating drug is added. Which concept best explains the urgent risk?
choices: A pharmacodynamic interaction may produce additive central nervous system depression
Only pharmacokinetic interactions can cause adverse effects
Unchanged drug concentrations guarantee no combined effect
Multiple sedating medications always cancel one another
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamic interactions can amplify a shared physiologic effect without changing measured drug concentrations. Marked sedation and respiratory depression require immediate assessment and response.
